lead: A car needs more than one kind of network. A door switch sends a few bits now and then; steering and damping need guaranteed timing; cameras and maps need high bandwidth. LIN is a cheap single-wire master-slave bus for body switches. FlexRay is a dual-channel time-triggered bus for x-by-wire. Automotive Ethernet is a switched high-bandwidth backbone. Each fills a niche, and they often meet through a gateway. This chapter explains how each bus works, what it costs, and where it is used.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for why buses replace point-to-point wiring, and Chapter 6.2 for CAN's arbitration and frame ideas.

blocks.text: LIN (Local Interconnect Network) is a low-cost bus for body electronics: door switches, mirrors, wipers, seat motors and climate flaps. It uses one wire for data, with a ground return, and 12 V signal levels. One master node polls up to 15 slave nodes. The master stores a schedule table: a list of headers to send in order. A header names the slave or signal to be exchanged. The addressed slave fills the data field; other slaves listen and may use the same data. This polling makes LIN predictable without arbitration.

items: Break: a long low pulse that wakes slaves for the frame.
Sync: a fixed byte so slaves can measure bit time.
Protected identifier: 6 identifier bits plus 2 parity bits.
Checksum: covers the data; enhanced checksum also covers the identifier.

blocks.text: LIN runs at 1 to 20 kbit/s; 19.2 kbit/s is common. A master can put the bus to sleep with a sleep command. A wake pulse or a dominant level wakes the cluster. LIN is not multi-master: only the master starts frames. Use LIN when cost and wire count matter more than speed. For engine and chassis signals, see CAN.

sections.h3: FlexRay: fixed slots on two channels

blocks.text: FlexRay is a time-triggered bus for systems where a late message is a fault: steer-by-wire, active suspension, brake and chassis control. It has two independent channels, A and B, each at 10 Mbit/s. A node may send on both channels for redundancy, or split traffic. The bus can form a star, a bus or a hybrid, so one broken wire need not stop communication. FlexRay is deterministic: every message has a fixed slot in a repeating communication cycle.

items: Static segment: TDMA (time-division multiple access). Fixed-length slots repeat in the same order; each slot belongs to one node, with no arbitration and no collisions.
Dynamic segment: FTDMA (flexible TDMA). Slots are numbered; a node sends only if it has data, so short frames leave time for later slots.
Symbol window: carries control symbols such as startup and wakeup.
Network idle time: lets nodes correct clocks and compute the next cycle.

blocks.text: Cycle length and slot size are set at design time. The static segment is the hard real-time part; the dynamic segment handles less regular traffic. Do not call FlexRay purely event-driven: its core guarantee comes from time-triggered static slots.

Automotive Ethernet brings switched, high-bandwidth networking to the car. 100BASE-T1 gives 100 Mbit/s over one unshielded twisted pair; 1000BASE-T1 gives 1 Gbit/s over one pair. Office Ethernet needed four pairs, which is too heavy and costly for a car. The physical layer uses full duplex on a single pair, so there is no collision domain. Nodes connect to a switch, making a star. A switch forwards frames only to the port that needs them, so several conversations can run at once.

Ethernet is used for cameras, radar, lidar, infotainment, diagnostics and the central backbone. VLANs (virtual local area networks) tag frames so one physical switch can carry separate traffic for safety, body and infotainment. SOME/IP (Scalable service-Oriented MiddlewarE over IP) lets ECUs call services by name rather than fixed signal addresses. AVB and TSN (Time-Sensitive Networking) add time synchronisation and scheduled traffic so audio and control frames get bounded latency. 10BASE-T1S is a 10 Mbit/s single-pair standard for short zonal links that can share a multidrop segment.
Ethernet does not replace LIN or CAN everywhere. A door switch does not need 100 Mbit/s. A gateway translates between buses. Use Ethernet where bandwidth or service-style communication is needed.

examples.question: A 1000-byte payload must cross the car. How long does it take on 100 Mbit/s automotive Ethernet and on a 20 kbit/s LIN bus? Ignore protocol overhead.
steps: Ethernet time = 8000 bit ÷ (100 × 10⁶ bit/s) = 8 × 10⁻⁵ s = 80 µs.
LIN time = 8000 bit ÷ (20 × 10³ bit/s) = 0.4 s = 400 ms.
examples.answer: The 1000-byte payload is 8000 bits; it takes 80 µs on 100 Mbit/s Ethernet and 400 ms on 20 kbit/s LIN, so Ethernet is 5000 times faster here.
examples.check:
payload_bytes = 1000
bits_per_byte = 8
payload_bits = payload_bytes * bits_per_byte
eth_rate = 100e6
lin_rate = 20e3
eth_time_s = payload_bits / eth_rate
lin_time_s = payload_bits / lin_rate
eth_time_us = eth_time_s * 1e6
lin_time_ms = lin_time_s * 1e3
ratio = lin_time_s / eth_time_s
print(payload_bits)
print(eth_time_us)
print(lin_time_ms)
print(ratio)

traps: LIN is not multi-master. One master polls up to 15 slaves; a slave never starts a frame on its own.
FlexRay's static segment is time-triggered TDMA. Do not call FlexRay purely event-driven; only the dynamic segment is flexible.
100BASE-T1 and 1000BASE-T1 use one twisted pair, not the four pairs of office Ethernet. The wire count 2 means the two wires in that pair.
Automotive Ethernet does not make CAN or LIN obsolete. A gateway joins them; cost and determinism still decide the choice.
A LIN frame's protected identifier is 6 identifier bits plus 2 parity bits, not a full 8-bit ID. Do not confuse it with a CAN identifier.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of LIN slaves under one master, and what is LIN's usual bit-rate range?
quiz.a: Up to 15 slaves under one master; 1 to 20 kbit/s, often 19.2 kbit/s.

quiz.q: Why does LIN use a schedule table instead of arbitration?
quiz.a: The master polls in a fixed order, so nodes cannot collide. Slaves need no arbitration hardware, which keeps cost low, and the polling order gives predictable latency.

quiz.q: A LIN frame carries 8 data bytes at 19.2 kbit/s. Ignoring header and checksum, what is the raw data time?
Why is FlexRay's static segment suitable for steer-by-wire?
quiz.a: Fixed TDMA slots repeat every cycle, so each critical message has a guaranteed time and no arbitration delay. Two channels can duplicate the data, and a missing or late slot is detectable.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of a FlexRay communication cycle.
quiz.a: Static segment, dynamic segment, symbol window, network idle time.

quiz.q: What does a switch do in automotive Ethernet?
quiz.a: It forwards a frame only to the port that leads to the destination. Multiple full-duplex conversations can run at once, and collisions do not occur.

quiz.q: A 2000-byte camera frame crosses 1000 Mbit/s Ethernet. Ignoring overhead, what is the time?
Why use 10BASE-T1S instead of 100BASE-T1 for a door cluster?
quiz.a: 10BASE-T1S is slower but supports a short multidrop segment with a simpler physical layer, so several small nodes share one link. 100BASE-T1 is point-to-point switched and costs more per node.

beyond: Not for the exam. Automotive Ethernet is moving from a diagnostic and camera link to a zonal backbone, where small switches sit near groups of sensors. TSN standards add scheduled traffic and time sync for safety-critical control. 10BASE-T1S brings Ethernet to short multidrop links that used to be CAN or LIN. SOME/IP and service-oriented design change how ECUs are updated and secured. Search next for IEEE 802.1AS time sync, TSN traffic shaping, and automotive Ethernet switch security.
